reviewer.summary: All nine planned claims are addressed, and the reported estimates and intervals match the cited Stage 2 evidence to rounding. The report clearly presents the null and inconclusive results and avoids causal claims. Before release, narrow the wording about negative scores and early attention to match what was measured.

issues.problem: The summary says, “That means more later publications cited each work alongside at least one of its references than cited it without any of them.” The phrase “each work” makes the result sound universal. F12 shows that 77.6% of ten-author works and 88.1% of works with 51–100 authors scored below zero, not all of them.
issues.fix: Replace it with: “For a work that scored below zero, more later publications cited it alongside at least one of its references than cited it without any of them.”

issues.problem: “The largest teams drew early attention, as in the original study” states a broader replication than the timing analysis supports. The clearest result is a larger first-full-year share among works cited in either of the first two full calendar years, not an unconditional finding about how soon large-team work receives attention.
issues.fix: Replace it with: “Among works cited in either of the first two full calendar years, teams of 51–100 authors received a larger share of those citations in the first full year than solo authors did. The ten-author comparison was inconclusive, and the data cannot test long-delayed recognition.”

issues.problem: “We sorted OpenAlex record numbers and drew randomly without replacement within groups, using PCG64 with seed 42” can be read as a numeric sort. J5 orders the string work IDs, and sorting numerically could change the seeded sample.
issues.fix: Write: “We sorted the OpenAlex work IDs as strings and drew randomly without replacement within groups, using PCG64 with seed 42.”

issues.problem: The summary sentence “They cited newer and generally more cited sources” does not identify the comparisons shown and can be read as a trend across all team sizes.
issues.fix: Write: “Compared with solo works, works with 10 or 51–100 authors cited newer and generally more highly cited references.”

issues.problem: The heading “What the original study asked” and its paragraph appear twice in succession.
issues.fix: Delete the second copy of the heading and paragraph.

reader.summary: The report is mostly easy to follow, and the worked example makes the disruption score concrete. The main revisions are to distinguish the two citation checks, say which works enter the ranking, and make clear that the summary’s description of negative scores applies only to works that scored below zero.

issues.problem: “A larger share of their works scored below zero. That means more later publications cited each work alongside at least one of its references than cited it without any of them.” The phrase “each work” makes the main result sound as though it applies to every work by a larger team, not just those with negative scores.
issues.fix: A larger share of works by larger teams had a negative disruption score. For a work with a negative score, more later publications cited it together with at least one of its references than cited it without citing any of its references.

issues.problem: “It also needed any one of three citation records in our copy of OpenAlex: a positive total citation count, a citation in a later calendar year through 2026, or a recorded citing work published after it.” The last two conditions sound like the same test. One uses a yearly count; the other uses a link to an individual citing work.
issues.fix: Our copy of OpenAlex also had to show at least one of three things: a total citation count above zero, a citation count above zero for a later calendar year through 2026, or a link to a citing work published after the sampled work, even in the same calendar year.

issues.problem: “We ranked each work among all eligible sampled works from its publication year, including the work itself.” The report has already described two eligibility checks. The reader needs to know which one determines the group used to calculate the main rank.
issues.fix: For the main analysis, we ranked each work against sampled works from the same publication year that were themselves cited during the period being analysed. The comparison included the work being ranked.

issues.problem: In the appendix, “Fit gaps” is an unexplained name for a model check.
issues.fix: We measured how far the models’ predictions were from the observed values. We did not use those differences as formal tests.

issues.problem: “For reviews alone, the trend was inconclusive under either eligibility rule. The difference between the two trends was inconclusive when works had to be cited themselves. When we also included works with only their references cited, the interval for the difference narrowly excluded zero.” The last sentence gives the reader the uncertainty but not which type of work had the steeper estimated decline.
issues.fix: For reviews, neither rule showed clearly whether rank rose or fell with team size. When we required a citation to the work itself, we could not tell whether the trends for articles and reviews differed. When we also included works with only their references cited, the estimated decline was steeper for articles, but the interval for the difference only just excluded zero.

issues.problem: “Each plotted reference gets the weight of the work listing it, so longer lists contribute more. We also compared each work’s average reference age using sampling weights.” The main text does not say whether reference age is measured at publication or when the data were collected.
issues.fix: We measured a reference’s age as the difference between its publication year and that of the work listing it. In the figure, each reference carries the sampling weight of the work that lists it, so longer lists contribute more. We also averaged reference ages within each work and used sampling weights to compare those averages.

issues.problem: “The curves show observed lists, not models. The age model assumes that raising the age cutoff by one year reduces the share of older references by the same fraction each time. The fitted share fell faster for ten-author than solo works.” “Observed lists” and “the fitted share fell faster” make readers work out what was counted and what the model found.
issues.fix: The curves show the references we counted. The age model assumes that raising the age cutoff by one year reduces the share of references older than that cutoff by the same fraction each time. That fraction was larger for works with ten authors than for solo works.

issues.problem: “We also calculated each work’s share arriving in the publication year, counting citations through the second full calendar year.” The reader has to infer that the denominator includes citations from the publication year itself as well as the next two years.
issues.fix: For each work, we counted citations from publication through the end of the second full calendar year after publication. We then calculated what share arrived in the publication year itself.

issues.problem: “Authors qualified if they had a recorded Columbia affiliation on eligible works with different team sizes. We counted each work under every author who qualified, splitting its sampling weight among them.” “Eligible works” and “counted each work under” obscure how authors entered the comparison and what happened when several on one work qualified.
issues.fix: An author qualified if they listed a Columbia affiliation on at least two works with different team sizes that were themselves cited in the main period. A work entered the comparison once for each qualifying author, with its sampling weight divided among those entries.

issues.problem: “The estimated trend was downward in 14 of 20 fields, or 70%, with a 95% interval of 55% to 80%. All 20 fields contained 6,074 works. For subfields, 24 of 34 had downward estimates, or 71%, with an interval of 53% to 76%. All qualifying subfields contained 3,601 works. Many individual intervals allowed no change or a rise.” The work counts can read as counts for each group rather than totals. The last sentence also switches from uncertainty about the share of groups to uncertainty about each group’s trend without saying so.
issues.fix: Across 20 qualifying fields with 6,074 works in total, 14 fields had estimated declines: 70%, with a 95% interval of 55% to 80%. Across 34 qualifying subfields with 3,601 works in total, 24 had estimated declines: 71%, with an interval of 53% to 76%. In many individual groups, the data were also consistent with no change or a rise.

issues.problem: “For most intervals we repeatedly drew from the original sample within each team-size group, allowing repeats. This is called a bootstrap. The middle 95% of the recalculated values gives the confidence interval for one estimate.” The text jumps from drawing works to “recalculated values” without saying that the same estimate is recalculated after each draw.
issues.fix: To measure sampling uncertainty for most estimates, we repeatedly drew works within each team-size group, allowing the same work to be drawn more than once. After each draw we recalculated the estimate. This procedure is called a bootstrap. We report the middle 95% of those estimates as the confidence interval.

issues.problem: “## What the original study asked” and its paragraph appear twice in a row.
issues.fix: Keep the first copy of the section and delete the second.

reviewer.summary: The report can be released as is. It addresses all nine planned claims, and the reported estimates, intervals, and counts agree with the cited Stage 2 evidence to rounding. It distinguishes the overall local association from the stronger original claims that were inconclusive or not testable, and it does not interpret the association as causal.

issues.problem: In “Of 55,371 Columbia-linked works, 10,720 had no usable reference and a recorded count of zero,” readers could mistake the recorded count for a citation count. Some of those works did have recorded citations.
issues.fix: Write: “Of the 55,371 Columbia-linked works in the snapshot, 10,720 had no usable reference link and a recorded reference count of zero.”

issues.problem: “The original study found that large teams drew early attention and that small teams and disruptive work gained recognition later” omits the brief’s qualification that some works never gained recognition. The local timing paragraph also leaves implicit which window supplied the positive and negative disruption scores.
issues.fix: Say that large-team work tended to draw attention sooner, while delayed recognition was more common for small-team and disruptive work. In “We compared works with negative and positive scores,” add “as measured in the main citation window.”

issues.problem: The C9 label “Partly testable” does not immediately distinguish the descriptive acknowledgment analysis from a reproduction of the original funding comparison.
issues.fix: Use “Original comparisons not testable; acknowledgment analysis is descriptive” in the funding section and summary table. When describing the original result, specify that Nobel-winning papers were unusually disruptive.

reader.summary: The report is mostly easy to follow, and the worked example makes the disruption score concrete. The two main revisions are to state what was averaged in the early-citation and reference-age comparisons. Most other fixes replace shorthand with the quantity or comparison it refers to.

issues.problem: “The weighted average first-full-year share was 5.23 percentage points higher for teams of 51 to 100 than for solo works.” It is not clear whether the authors calculated a share for each work and averaged those shares, or pooled citations across each team-size group. Those methods give different weight to highly cited works.
issues.fix: For each work, we calculated what share of its citations in the first two full calendar years came in the first of those years. We then averaged those shares using the sampling weights. The average was 5.23 percentage points higher for works with 51 to 100 authors than for solo works.

issues.problem: “Among works themselves cited in the main window, references in ten-author works were 5.20 years newer than in solo works, with a 95% interval of 4.41 to 6.05 years newer among 1,221 works.” The paragraph describes two ways to count references, but the result does not say which one it uses.
issues.fix: We first calculated the average reference age for each work, then compared those averages using the sampling weights. Among 1,221 works cited in the main window, references in ten-author works were 5.20 years newer on this measure than references in solo works, with a 95% interval of 4.41 to 6.05 years newer.

issues.problem: “On the scale from 0 to 100, the rank is the percentage of total sampling weight below its score plus half the percentage tied at its score. The tied weight includes the work’s own weight.” The wording makes it sound as though the weights, rather than the works’ scores, are below or tied.
issues.fix: To get a rank from 0 to 100, add the weights of works with lower scores and half the weights of works with the same score, including the work itself. Express that sum as a percentage of the total weight for the year.

issues.problem: “Including works that scored zero because only their references were cited in the relevant window barely changed the main team-size result, though the appendix shows differences for the shorter window and for reviews compared with articles.” The sentence sends readers to the appendix without saying how the results differed.
issues.fix: Including works whose references were cited but that were not themselves cited barely changed the main decline in rank with team size. It made the estimated decline steeper in the shorter window. With these works included, the interval for the difference between the article and review trends just excluded zero.

issues.problem: “Reviews and the model of highly cited references gave inconclusive results.” The summary does not say what either comparison was meant to establish.
issues.fix: We could not tell whether reviews’ disruption ranks rose or fell with team size, or whether very high citation counts became rarer at different rates among references cited by solo and ten-author works.

issues.problem: “After each draw we recalculated the estimate.” This can sound as though the estimate was recalculated after drawing one work. Later in the paragraph, “the largest group, where we drew every work” can mean the group with the most works rather than the group with the largest teams.
issues.fix: After drawing a new sample from the original sample, we recalculated the estimate. For the last sentence, write: We used the same method even for teams of 51 to 100 authors, although we had originally sampled every eligible work in that group.

issues.problem: “Across 20 qualifying fields with 6,074 works in total, 14 fields had estimated declines: 70%, with a 95% interval of 55% to 80%. Across 34 qualifying subfields with 3,601 works in total, 24 had estimated declines: 71%, with an interval of 53% to 76%.” It is not immediately clear why the percentages have intervals when the numbers of fields and subfields are fixed.
issues.fix: Add after these results: Each time we drew a new sample, we kept the same fields and subfields but recalculated their trends. The intervals show how the percentage with a decline varied across those draws.

issues.problem: “Our copy of OpenAlex also had to show at least one of three things: a total citation count above zero, a citation count above zero for a later calendar year through 2026, or a link to a citing work published after the sampled work, even in the same calendar year.” The three alternatives are hard to separate on a first reading, especially the two kinds of counts.
issues.fix: For sampling, we accepted any of three signs of a citation in our copy of OpenAlex: a positive overall count; a positive annual count for a year after publication, through 2026; or a link to a citing work published after the sampled work, including later in the same year.

issues.problem: “The first-full-year measure did not establish a difference by score. Some citations enter both scores and timing measures.” Both sentences rely on shorthand for quantities defined earlier.
issues.fix: Among citations in the first two full calendar years, works with positive and negative disruption scores did not clearly differ in the share received in the first year. Some of the same citations helped determine both the disruption score and when attention arrived.

issues.problem: “The cutoff sets which publication dates count; it does not reconstruct the index on that date.” The reader has to work out the distinction between a citing work’s publication date and the date OpenAlex recorded it.
issues.fix: The cutoff applies to when citing works were published, not to when OpenAlex recorded their citations.

reviewer.summary: The report is ready for release. Its estimates and intervals agree with the cited Stage 2 evidence, and it addresses all nine planned claims. It distinguishes the overall local association from findings that were inconclusive or not testable, and does not interpret the association as causal.

issues.problem: “We used the same method even for teams of 51 to 100 authors, although we had originally sampled every eligible work in that group.” This is accurate, but readers may mistake those bootstrap intervals for sampling uncertainty within the fixed OpenAlex frame.
issues.fix: Add that the bootstrap used no finite-population correction. For raw statistics within the 51–100-author group, the intervals describe variability under resampling, not uncertainty from selecting works in a group that was fully enumerated.

issues.problem: “The decline held within authors.” The methods identify the restricted sample, but the takeaway does not remind readers that the unadjusted slope was already smaller in that sample than in the full analysis.
issues.fix: Write: “The decline persisted after adjustment in the subset with within-author variation. In that same subset, the unadjusted decline was 1.73 points per doubling, compared with 3.48 points in the full 1–10-author analysis.”

issues.problem: “Original comparisons not testable.” This is accurate for C9’s original comparisons, but it makes the planned local funding-record analysis easy to miss in the status summary.
issues.fix: Use “Partly testable: local funding records only” in the section and summary table. Keep the distinction between recorded acknowledgment and verified funding status, and retain the list of original comparisons that could not be tested.

reader.summary: The main findings are easy to follow, and the report generally distinguishes estimates from conclusions. Two methods need clearer wording: how later works count toward the disruption score, and what it means to compare works by the same author. Most other revisions can be made by naming the rank, group, or comparison directly.

issues.problem: In the disruption-score definition, “Count each later work only once” leaves it unclear whether a work counted in the subtraction also counts in the total used for division. The definition also switches from “work” to “paper,” although the sample includes book chapters.
issues.fix: Sort later works into three groups: those that cite the sampled work without any of its references, those that cite it with at least one of its references, and those that cite only its references. Count each later work in just one group. Subtract the second count from the first, then divide by the total across all three groups. If all three counts are zero, there is no score.

issues.problem: “The link remained when comparing works by the same authors” can sound as though the works had identical author lists. The method compares works that share a qualifying author, not an entire team.
issues.fix: The link remained when we compared each qualifying author’s works. In the methods paragraph, say: “We compared works with different team sizes by each qualifying author, allowing average ranks to differ by publication year and main OpenAlex topic.”

issues.problem: “Larger teams generally ranked lower against works from the same year, but not at every size or in every field.” The summary has just mentioned both citation counts and disruption scores, so the reader has to infer which was ranked.
issues.fix: We ranked works by disruption score within each publication year. Works by larger teams generally ranked lower, but not at every team size or in every field.

issues.problem: “The least-cited group is below the 50th percentile. The middle group begins there and the top group begins at the 90th percentile. Ties share a rank. Weights determine the groups, so the lowest group need not contain half the sampled works.” The reader has to reconstruct the middle group’s upper limit and how the weights affect the cutoffs.
issues.fix: Within each publication year, we ranked works by citation count using the sampling weights. Tied counts share a rank. The least-cited group is below the 50th percentile, the middle group runs from the 50th to just below the 90th, and the top group starts at the 90th. Because the ranks are weighted, the lowest group need not contain half the sampled works.

issues.problem: “Neither eligibility rule showed clearly whether review ranks rose or fell with team size.” The two rules have not yet been named in this comparison.
issues.fix: We could not tell whether reviews ranked higher or lower as team size grew, whether we required a citation to the review itself or also included reviews with citations only to their references.

issues.problem: “We drew separately at each size from one to ten and for groups of 11 to 20, 21 to 50 and 51 to 100. A work counted for more if we drew a smaller fraction of its group. This is its sampling weight.” The reader has to supply what was drawn and infer how much more a work counted.
issues.fix: We randomly sampled works separately at each team size from one to ten and in three ranges: 11 to 20, 21 to 50, and 51 to 100. A work’s sampling weight was the number of eligible works in its group divided by the number we sampled.

issues.problem: “The citation model assumes that doubling a citation count reduces the predicted share with exactly that count by the same fraction each time.” This takes a second reading because the count doubles while the share falls, and the share refers to exactly that count, not that count or more.
issues.fix: The model predicts that the share of references with exactly 100 citations is smaller than the share with exactly 50. It assumes the same proportional drop from 100 to 200 citations. Among references with at least 50 citations, we could not tell whether that drop differed between solo and ten-author works.

issues.problem: “For each doubling of team size, the estimated change in rank was 2.73 points higher in the top tenth than in the least-cited half.” It is easy to read “higher” as a difference in ranks rather than a difference in how ranks changed.
issues.fix: For each doubling of team size, the rank was estimated to rise by 0.23 points in the most-cited tenth and fall by 2.50 points in the least-cited half. That is a 2.73-point difference in the estimated changes. The 95% interval ranged from 1.89 points lower to 6.00 points higher for the most-cited tenth, based on 3,734 works.

issues.problem: “Without this extra citation filter, the difference was 5.38 years, with an interval of 4.58 to 6.24 years among 1,249 works.” The reader has to look back to see which requirement was dropped and which team’s references were newer.
issues.fix: Without requiring a citation to the work itself in the main window, references in ten-author works were 5.38 years newer on average than those in solo works. The interval was 4.58 to 6.24 years, based on 1,249 works.

issues.problem: “We also counted citations from the day after publication through the end of the second full calendar year. We calculated the share that arrived in the publication year itself.” It is not explicit whether the share is calculated for each work or from pooled citations.
issues.fix: For each work, we also counted citations from the day after publication through the end of the second full calendar year. We calculated what share of that work’s citations in this period arrived before the end of its publication year.

issues.problem: “Per doubling, rank fell by an estimated 3.75 points without a recorded acknowledgment and rose by an estimated 0.52 points with one; only the decline was clear.” This makes the reader supply both what doubles and which rank changes.
issues.fix: For each doubling of team size, the estimated disruption rank fell by 3.75 points for works without a recorded funding acknowledgment and rose by 0.52 points for works with one. Only the decline was clear.

reviewer.summary: The reported estimates, intervals, and sample counts agree with the cited Stage 2 evidence. All nine claims are addressed, including the inconclusive high-impact and review results, the limited journal coverage, and the comparisons the data cannot test. The conclusions stay within the evidence and do not imply that adding authors causes a change in disruption.

issues.problem: The opening sentence, “Larger teams generally drew more citations in recent Columbia-linked research,” leaves the analysis population implicit. The methods and limitations make the restriction clear later.
issues.fix: Make the scope explicit up front: “Among sampled 2021–2024 Columbia-linked OpenAlex works cited at least once in the main window, larger teams generally received more citations.”

issues.problem: “The original study mostly reported ranks rather than raw scores” is accurate, but the contrast between the original ranking population and the reproduction’s within-year ranking is easy to miss.
issues.fix: State the difference directly: “The original study mostly reported percentiles across works. We instead calculated sampling-weighted percentiles within each publication year.”

issues.problem: “Partly testable: local funding records only” could be read as saying that the recorded-acknowledgment analysis directly tests part of the original policy comparison. The surrounding text correctly distinguishes the two.
issues.fix: Use “Original comparisons not testable; local funding-record comparison only” in both the section and the recap table.

reader.summary: The main findings are easy to follow, and the worked examples make the disruption score and rank understandable. The two most important fixes are to state in the main text that the simpler-score and funding trends cover only works with one to ten authors.

issues.problem: “For each doubling of team size, the estimated disruption rank fell by 3.75 points for works without a recorded funding acknowledgment and rose by 0.52 points for works with one. Only the decline was clear. The change was 4.26 points higher with an acknowledgment, with a 95% interval of 2.68 to 5.83 points higher among 6,210 works.” The main text does not say that this comparison is limited to works with one to ten authors. It can be read as a result for the full range of team sizes.
issues.fix: Among 6,210 works with one to ten authors, each doubling of team size was associated with a drop of 3.75 rank points for works without a recorded funding acknowledgment and a rise of 0.52 points for works with one. The data supported the decline but did not establish a rise. The estimated change was 4.26 points higher for works with an acknowledgment, with a 95% interval of 2.68 to 5.83 points higher.

issues.problem: “The simpler score counts the share of later works citing the sampled work that cite none of its references. It fell by 4.29 percentage points per doubling, with a 95% interval of 3.40 to 5.21 points of decline among 6,210 works.” The nested definition obscures which works go into the score, and the main text does not say which team sizes the result covers.
issues.fix: For each sampled work, we took the later works that cited it and calculated the percentage that cited none of its references. Among 6,210 works with one to ten authors, that percentage fell by 4.29 points per doubling of team size. The 95% interval was a decline of 3.40 to 5.21 percentage points.

issues.problem: “A larger share of works by larger teams scored below zero. For a work with a negative score, more later publications cited it alongside at least one of its references than cited it without any of them.” The summary gives the result before naming the score or saying what zero means.
issues.fix: A work scores below zero on disruption when more later publications cite it with at least one of its references than cite it without any. Works by larger teams more often scored below zero.

issues.problem: “We also required one of three signs of a citation in our copy of OpenAlex: a positive overall count; a positive annual count for a later calendar year, through 2026; or a link to a citing work published after the sampled work, including later in the same year.” It takes a second reading to distinguish this sampling rule from the later requirement to find a citing work within the analysis window.
issues.fix: To be eligible for sampling, a work needed at least one of three signs that it had been cited in our copy of OpenAlex: an overall count above zero, an annual count above zero for a later calendar year through 2026, or a link to a citing work published later, even in the same year. For the main disruption analysis, we separately checked for a citing work published within the window.

issues.problem: “The citation model assumes the same proportional drop in the share of references from exactly 50 to exactly 100 citations as from exactly 100 to exactly 200 citations.” The wording makes the numbers look like ranges rather than three exact counts that illustrate a general rule.
issues.fix: The model assumes that each doubling of the citation count reduces the share of references with exactly that count by the same fraction. For example, the fraction lost from 50 to 100 citations is the same as from 100 to 200.

issues.problem: “For raw statistics on teams of 51 to 100, the intervals show variation across repeat draws, not uncertainty from the original selection: we sampled every eligible work in that group.” It is unclear which results count as “raw statistics.”
issues.fix: For statistics based only on teams of 51 to 100 authors, such as their median citation count, the intervals show how estimates vary when we draw those works again. There was no uncertainty about which eligible works we picked: we picked them all.

issues.problem: “The median is the middle count when works are ordered by citations.” This definition suggests that each sampled work counts equally, although the reported medians use sampling weights.
issues.fix: The median is the citation count at the halfway point after ordering works by citation count and counting each work according to its sampling weight.

issues.problem: “The least-cited group is below the 50th percentile, the middle group runs from the 50th to just below the 90th, and the top group starts at the 90th.” The main text switches from “rank” to “percentile” without saying that these cutoffs are ranks on the same kind of scale, but for citation counts rather than disruption scores.
issues.fix: On the 0 to 100 citation-rank scale, the least-cited group is below 50, the middle group starts at 50 and stops just before 90, and the top group starts at 90.

issues.problem: “The estimated rise in the top tenth and decline in the least-cited half were 2.73 points apart per doubling. The 95% interval for the difference, based on 3,734 works, ranged from 1.89 points lower to 6.00 points higher for the change in the top tenth. We could not tell which group had the steeper decline.” The reader has to work out which change is being subtracted from which, and the last sentence suggests that both groups declined.
issues.fix: Per doubling of team size, the estimated change in rank was 2.73 points higher in the top tenth than in the least-cited half. Based on 3,734 works, the 95% interval ranged from 1.89 points lower to 6.00 points higher. We could not establish that the trends differed.

issues.problem: “We compared works with different team sizes by each qualifying author, allowing average ranks to differ by publication year and main OpenAlex topic.” The placement of “by each qualifying author” makes the comparison hard to parse.
issues.fix: For each qualifying author, we compared the disruption ranks of their works with different team sizes. We accounted for differences in average rank by publication year and by the main topic OpenAlex assigned to each work.

issues.problem: “Among works cited in either of the first two full calendar years after publication, works with 51 to 100 authors received a larger share of those citations in the first year, on average, than solo works did.” The sentence asks readers to track which works were included, which years count and which teams were compared all at once.
issues.fix: We looked at works cited in the first or second full calendar year after publication. On average, works with 51 to 100 authors received a greater share of those citations in the first full year than solo works did.

reviewer.summary: The reported estimates, intervals and counts match the cited evidence, and all nine planned claims have clear outcomes. The report distinguishes the overall local pattern from a steady decline, gives the inconclusive high-impact and review results, and explains which original claims the Columbia sample cannot test. The remaining edits clarify the timing sample and the interpretation of the author model; neither changes the findings.

issues.problem: In the timing section, “For each work, we also counted citations from the day after publication through the end of the second full calendar year” can sound as though the publication-year analysis reused the first-full-year analysis sample. The two measures use different citation eligibility rules.
issues.fix: Replace that sentence with: “For the separate publication-year analysis, a work qualified if it had at least one citation from the day after publication through the end of the second full calendar year, even if all its citations arrived in the publication year.”

issues.problem: The heading “The link held when we compared each qualifying author’s works” could be read as saying the decline held for every qualifying author. The model estimates one pooled association from within-author comparisons.
issues.fix: Use the heading “The decline persisted in the pooled within-author analysis.”

reader.summary: The main findings are readable, but the report should distinguish citation evidence used for sampling from the citation requirement for analysis. It should also state which works enter each ranking and consistently distinguish disruption rank from citation rank.

issues.problem: “For the main disruption analysis, we separately checked for a later work citing the sampled work within the citation window.” This does not say that finding a later citing work was a requirement for the main analysis, not just a check on the citation evidence used for sampling.
issues.fix: For the main analysis, a sampled work qualified only if we found a work anywhere in OpenAlex that cited it and was published after it, through 23 November 2026. For the shorter analysis, the cutoff was 31 December of the second calendar year after publication. Works from 2024 had not had that much follow-up, so we excluded them from the shorter analysis.

issues.problem: “Express that sum as a percentage of the total eligible weight for the year.” After the report has used “eligible” for entry into the sample, it is unclear whether this total includes all works eligible for sampling or only sampled works cited within the window.
issues.fix: Divide that sum by the total weight of sampled works from the same publication year that were cited in the window, and express the result as a percentage.

issues.problem: “The least-cited group fell by 2.50 rank points per doubling, with a 95% interval of 1.64 to 3.39 points of decline among 3,277 works. The middle result was inconclusive. The top estimate was a rise of 0.23 points; its interval ran from a decline of 4.33 to a rise of 3.37 points among 457 works.” The preceding paragraph explains citation ranks, so the reader has to infer that these results concern disruption rank and that the doubling is in team size.
issues.fix: In the least-cited group, disruption rank fell by an estimated 2.50 points per doubling of team size. The 95% interval was a fall of 1.64 to 3.39 points, based on 3,277 works. The middle group showed no clear rise or fall. In the most-cited group, the estimated change per doubling was a rise of 0.23 points, with an interval from a fall of 4.33 to a rise of 3.37 points, based on 457 works.

issues.problem: “We ranked them within each publication year, separately for each window.” This leaves the main step in the window comparison implicit: what was ranked, and whether each ranking used the same set of works.
issues.fix: For each window, we recalculated the disruption scores of these same works and ranked them against one another within each publication year.

issues.problem: “Among sampled Columbia-linked works published from 2021 through 2024 in OpenAlex and cited in the main window, larger teams generally received more citations.” The opening packs in two terms not yet explained, and “published … in OpenAlex” makes the index sound like the publisher.
issues.fix: In our OpenAlex sample, larger teams generally received more citations. This comparison covered works published from 2021 through 2024 with at least one Columbia-affiliated author and at least one later work citing them by 23 November 2026.

issues.problem: “Including works whose references were cited but that were not themselves cited barely changed the main decline in rank with team size. It made the estimated decline steeper in the shorter window.” It is unclear whether “steeper” means steeper than in the main window or steeper than under the original rule for the shorter window.
issues.fix: We also included works that were not themselves cited but had at least one cited reference. Compared with requiring a citation to the work itself, this rule barely changed the estimated decline in disruption rank in the main window and made the decline steeper in the shorter window.

issues.problem: “The citation model assumes that each doubling of the citation count reduces the predicted share of references with exactly that count by the same fraction. For example, the fraction lost when comparing exactly 50 citations with exactly 100 is the same as when comparing exactly 100 with exactly 200.” “The fraction lost” sounds as though references were removed, rather than that references with higher counts were predicted to be less common.
issues.fix: The model predicts that references with exactly 100 citations are less common than those with exactly 50 by the same fraction that references with exactly 200 citations are less common than those with exactly 100.

issues.problem: “For a statistic based only on teams of 51 to 100 authors, such as their median citation count, the interval shows variation across repeat draws. There was no uncertainty about which eligible works we picked in that group: we picked them all.” The reason for the interval is easier to follow if the report first says that the actual sample included the whole group.
issues.fix: We sampled every eligible work by teams of 51 to 100 authors. For estimates such as that group’s median citation count, the interval shows how much the estimate varied across repeat draws with replacement, not uncertainty about which eligible works we originally sampled.

issues.problem: “A work’s sampling weight was the number of eligible works in its group divided by the number we sampled.” The second count could mean the number sampled overall rather than the number sampled in that group.
issues.fix: Within each team-size group, we divided the number of eligible works by the number sampled in that group. Each sampled work got that weight.

issues.problem: “The fitted age difference agreed in direction; the citation model comparison was inconclusive.” In the comparison table, “fitted age difference” could mean the gap in average reference age, but it refers to how quickly older references became less common.
issues.fix: The age model estimated that older references became rarer faster in ten-author works than in solo works. The citation model did not show a clear difference in how quickly highly cited references became rarer.
